items.goal: Sort the whole filtered catalog on the server: the v2 GET /api/catalog/items gets an optional sort (name-asc|name-desc|price-asc|price-desc) applied before paging, CatalogService and Catalog.razor pass a ?sort= query parameter through, and catalog-sort.js navigates to the sorted URL (page reset, localStorage pref restored by URL replace when ?sort is missing) instead of reordering cards.
items.modelReason: Straightforward cross-layer change; the JS and URL state handling needs care but no hard design work.
items.verifyReason: The bug is visible in the browser: sorted order across catalog pages and the Sort control's persisted state.

alternatives.option: Keep client-side sort but fetch all items into the WebApp and page in memory
alternatives.reason: Moves paging out of the API and loads the whole catalog per request; breaks the count/paging contract.

alternatives.option: Persist the sort in a cookie read during SSR instead of a query param
alternatives.reason: Needs HttpContext plumbing in static SSR; the query param composes with the existing GetUriWithQueryParameter links for free.

items.reason: Straightforward cross-layer change; the JS and URL state handling needs care but no hard design work.

subject: implementer
reason: Sorting moved to Catalog.API v2 GetAllItems before Skip/Take, with Name/Id tie-breaks and the count query unchanged, so the whole filtered catalog is in order across pages with the same counts and page count. The WebApp carries `sort` in the URL, keeps it in the page/filter links (GetUriWithQueryParameter(s)), renders the selected option on the server and restores the stored choice after reload; the v2 OpenAPI doc is regenerated and ICatalogService/HybridApp are untouched.

items.reason: When sync() restores a stored non-default sort on a URL without `sort`, sortedUrl() also removes `page`, so a bookmarked /?page=3 opens page 1.
items.fix: Pass a flag to sortedUrl so it only removes `page` when the user picks a new sort, not when sync() restores a stored one.

items.reason: On a first load without `sort` and a stored non-default sort, location.replace loads the catalog a second time; the default order shows briefly before the sorted one.
items.fix: Acceptable for now; if it matters, have the server read the preference (for example from a cookie) instead of reloading on the client.

items.reason: data-sort-name/data-sort-price attributes are no longer read by any script (dead markup).

items.title: Price: Low to High puts the cheapest products on page 1 and continues on page 2
covers: Steps to Reproduce 1-3
Expected: page 1 starts with the cheapest product; no product on a later page costs less
Acceptance criterion
items.reason: This is the bug report replayed as written: before the fix, page 1 showed $79.99 to $249.99 and page 2 started at $59.99. It must be e2e because the defect was in how the WebApp applied the sort (client-side reorder of one page), which an API test alone cannot catch.

items.title: Price: High to Low orders the whole catalog from the most expensive product
covers: Expected: Price: High to Low works the same way in its own order
items.reason: The ticket names "Price: High to Low" as broken in the same way. A separate case is needed because it is a different sort direction and tie-break (price descending, then name ascending), and the last page proves the cheapest products end the catalog, not just page 1.

items.title: Name: Z to A orders the whole catalog, ending with Adventurer GPS Watch on the last page
covers: Expected: Name: Z to A works the same way in its own order
items.reason: "Name: Z to A" had the same per-page defect. The first page and the last page together prove the order spans the whole catalog: before the fix, page 1 only showed the A-names reversed and the last page could not end with "Adventurer GPS Watch".

items.title: Name: A to Z stays the default order with no sort in the URL
covers: Expected: Name: A to Z stays as it is today
items.reason: The ticket requires the default order to stay as it is. The fix moves sorting into the URL, so switching back to "Name: A to Z" must return to the plain catalog URL and today's page 1; a regression here would change the landing page for every visitor.

items.title: Price sort applies to the filtered result across its pages
covers: Expected: whole catalog with the active brand filter in price order across its pages
Expected: the filters do not change
items.reason: The ticket says the order applies to the catalog "with the active brand and type filters". Gravitator has 11 items (2 pages) with its two 699.00 skis last, so a per-page reorder or a sort that drops the filter would show a wrong first or second page.

items.title: Changing a filter keeps the chosen sort and sorts the new result
covers: Expected: whole catalog with the active type filter in price order
Expected: the chosen sort stays selected
items.reason: Sort now lives in the URL, so filter links must carry it; if they dropped `sort`, picking a type after choosing a sort would silently return to Name: A to Z. This is the type-filter half of "with the active brand and type filters" and is separate from TC-BUG-40-05, where the filter was chosen before the sort.

items.title: Sorting does not change the product count, filter counts, page count or cards per page
covers: Expected: product count, filters and their counts, number of pages unchanged; each page still shows 9 products
items.reason: The ticket explicitly requires the count, filter counts and paging to be unaffected by the sort. The fix touches the items query and the page links, so a sort that leaked into the count or facet query would change these numbers; the e2e layer is where all four numbers are visible together.

items.title: The chosen sort stays selected on a later page and after a reload
covers: Expected: the chosen sort stays selected on every page and after a reload
items.reason: Before the fix the selected label was restored by script; now it is rendered from `?sort`. A reload of a deep page must render the same label, `aria-selected` state and server-sorted cards, or the user sees a mismatch between the control and the order.

items.title: Returning to the catalog without a sort restores the stored sort
covers: Expected: the chosen sort stays selected ... as it does today (stored preference)
Implementation Notes: sync replaces the URL with the stored sort when ?sort is missing; key aw.catalog.sort.v1 kept
items.reason: Today the sort choice persists across visits through localStorage key `aw.catalog.sort.v1`. With sorting moved to the URL, opening plain `/` must restore that choice and also apply it on the server; otherwise the label would say "Price: Low to High" over a name-ordered page, which is this bug again.

items.title: Choosing a sort on page 3 starts the sorted catalog at page 1
covers: Expected: page 1 starts with the cheapest product
Implementation Notes: choosing a sort resets to page 1
items.reason: A user often sorts after paging. If the new sort kept `page=3`, the user would land in the middle of the price order and never see the cheapest product, which is the visible symptom of this bug. Separate from TC-BUG-40-01, which starts on page 1.

items.title: API: price-asc orders all 101 items across every page
covers: Expected: whole catalog in price order across its pages; no product on a later page costs less
Expected: product count unchanged; each page shows 9 products
Implementation Notes: sort applied before Skip/Take; price ties broken by Name then Id
items.reason: "No product on a later page costs less than a product on an earlier page" is a statement about all 12 pages; only a page-by-page walk proves it, and that is cheap and exact against the API the WebApp now calls. It also proves no item is repeated or skipped between pages, which a non-deterministic tie-break would break (ten items cost 79.99).

items.title: API: price-desc orders all 101 items across every page
covers: Expected: Price: High to Low works the same way in its own order
Implementation Notes: price-desc ties broken by Name then Id
items.reason: Same whole-catalog guarantee as TC-BUG-40-11 for the opposite direction; a separate case because descending price uses its own ordering expression and tie-break (name ascending), which could be wired wrong independently.

items.title: API: name-desc orders all 101 items across every page
covers: Expected: Name: Z to A works the same way in its own order
Implementation Notes: name sorts break ties by Id
items.reason: "Name: Z to A" must span the whole catalog. Asserting the first and last pages plus completeness proves the order is applied before paging; full name-by-name comparison is avoided because it depends on database collation (see Open questions).

items.title: API: no sort and name-asc return today's default order
covers: Expected: Name: A to Z stays as it is today
Implementation Notes: name-asc is the default; the default sort sends no sort parameter
items.reason: The WebApp sends no `sort` for "Name: A to Z", and every other caller of v2 `/items` sends none either, so the parameterless order must stay exactly as before; `sort=name-asc` must mean the same thing. Duplicate names (items 17 and 74, both "Apex Climbing Harness") check the Id tie-break that keeps paging stable.

items.title: API: sort with brand and type filters orders only the filtered items and keeps their count
covers: Expected: whole catalog with the active brand filter in price order across its pages
Expected: product count unchanged by the sort
items.reason: The sort must combine with filters: filtered first, then sorted, then paged. The count query is separate from the sorted items query, so this also proves `count` reflects the filter and not the sort. API layer because it can compare the exact ids of both pages and the count with and without `sort`.

items.title: API: an unknown sort value falls back to the default order
covers: Implementation Notes: unknown sort values fall back to the default without error
items.reason: The `sort` value comes from a user-editable URL. The Implementation Notes state that an unknown value uses the default order without an error, so a hand-edited or stale link must still show the catalog instead of failing. Functional, because the fallback is in the API's sort switch.

subject: test-planner
reason: Every Expected bullet and the acceptance criterion are covered by exact, concrete e2e and functional cases, but TC-03 and TC-13 assert a page-1 name order (Venture 2022 Snowboard before Venture 2.0 40L Waterproof Duffel Bag) that holds only under ordinal collation, breaking the plan's own rule to assert only collation-stable positions.

items.reason: Page 1 expects 'Venture 2022 Snowboard' 8th and 'Venture 2.0 40L Waterproof Duffel Bag' 9th. Under a linguistic collation such as Postgres en_US.utf8, which mostly ignores spaces and punctuation, 'venture2040l...' sorts after 'venture2022...', so name-desc puts the Duffel Bag first. That contradicts the plan's open question, which says name cases assert only collation-stable positions. Assert positions 1-7 exactly and the last two as the set {Venture 2022 Snowboard, Venture 2.0 40L Waterproof Duffel Bag}, or name the collation the stack uses and assert that order.
items.subject: test-planner

items.reason: Page 0 data[*].id is asserted exactly as [30, 46, 1, 55, 11, 9, 33, 22, 67]; whether 22 (Venture 2022 Snowboard) comes before 67 (Venture 2.0 40L Waterproof Duffel Bag) depends on the database collation, the same issue as TC-03. Assert the first seven ids exactly and {22, 67} as a set in the last two places, or name the collation the fixture uses.
items.subject: test-planner

items.reason: "No product on a later page costs less than a product on an earlier page" is a statement about all 12 pages; only a page-by-page walk proves it, and that is cheap and exact against the API the WebApp now calls. It also proves no item is repeated or skipped between pages, which a non-deterministic tie-break would break (ten items cost 79.99).

items.title: API: price-desc orders all 101 items across every page
covers: Expected: Price: High to Low works the same way in its own order
Implementation Notes: price-desc ties broken by Name then Id
items.reason: Same whole-catalog guarantee as TC-BUG-40-11 for the opposite direction; a separate case because descending price uses its own ordering expression and tie-break (name ascending), which could be wired wrong independently.

items.title: API: name-desc orders all 101 items across every page
covers: Expected: Name: Z to A works the same way in its own order
Implementation Notes: name sorts break ties by Id
items.reason: "Name: Z to A" must span the whole catalog. Asserting the first and last pages plus completeness proves the order is applied before paging; full name-by-name comparison is avoided because it depends on database collation (see Open questions).

items.title: API: no sort and name-asc return today's default order
covers: Expected: Name: A to Z stays as it is today
Implementation Notes: name-asc is the default; the default sort sends no sort parameter
items.reason: The WebApp sends no `sort` for "Name: A to Z", and every other caller of v2 `/items` sends none either, so the parameterless order must stay exactly as before; `sort=name-asc` must mean the same thing. Duplicate names (items 17 and 74, both "Apex Climbing Harness") check the Id tie-break that keeps paging stable.

items.title: API: sort with brand and type filters orders only the filtered items and keeps their count
covers: Expected: whole catalog with the active brand filter in price order across its pages
Expected: product count unchanged by the sort
items.reason: The sort must combine with filters: filtered first, then sorted, then paged. The count query is separate from the sorted items query, so this also proves `count` reflects the filter and not the sort. API layer because it can compare the exact ids of both pages and the count with and without `sort`.

items.title: API: an unknown sort value falls back to the default order
covers: Implementation Notes: unknown sort values fall back to the default without error
items.reason: The `sort` value comes from a user-editable URL. The Implementation Notes state that an unknown value uses the default order without an error, so a hand-edited or stale link must still show the catalog instead of failing. Functional, because the fallback is in the API's sort switch.

subject: test-planner
reason: Every Expected bullet and step maps to concrete cases with exact ids, prices and URLs, and the functional cases walk all 12 pages. Two minor gaps: brand and type filters are never active together, and the e2e cases don't name the user.

items.reason: Expected bullet 1 says the order applies 'with the active brand and type filters', but brand (TC-05/15) and type (TC-06/15) are only tested on their own. Add a request or UI flow with both active (for example brand=2&type=3&sort=price-asc) asserting the exact ids in order and the count, and the order across pages if the result spans more than one.
items.subject: test-planner

items.reason: The project context requires e2e cases to name the seeded user; TC-01 to TC-10 don't. State that the catalog is browsed by an anonymous (not signed-in) visitor in each e2e case's Preconditions or in the plan index.

subject: test-automation
reason: All 16 cases are implemented faithfully: 6 functional tests assert exact ids, prices, counts and statuses against the real API, and 10 e2e tests assert exact URLs, sort labels, aria-selected, counts and card names and prices. Every UI keyframe I opened shows the asserted state. One point off for a factually wrong comment in TC-BUG-40-06 that claims the test departs from the case when it does not.

items.reason: The comment before the page-2 assertions says 'The case names Blizzard Rider Snowboard $299.99 as the first card' and justifies 'asserting the real order'. The case actually expects Raven Swift Snowboard $349.00 first and Blizzard Rider second, which is exactly what the test asserts. The misleading comment should be removed so the test does not look like it departs from the spec.
